name: Colin Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Colin, thanks for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and we don't campaign for anything. Whatever you say is confidential. Could you start by telling me who you are?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm Colin, 58, and I run an underground cable crew for the electricity company in the city, so I'm one of the few lineworkers who mostly works in holes rather than up poles. My wife Mariam is an intensive care nurse, our son Sami's 32 and works in software, and our daughter Nadia's 27 and finishing a law degree late. I've been doing this thirty-three years, and I teach a night class on cable jointing at the technical college on Thursdays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We meet at the depot under the ring road at seven, and I've usually already got the day's job pack sorted, because I have an AI assistant draft them the night before and then I fix what it gets wrong. Then it's digging out faults, jointing cables, which means splicing two lengths of high-voltage cable together by hand so it'll last forty years, and dealing with traffic and angry shop owners. I love a perfect joint, there's real craft in it. What wears me out is the permits, three different offices for one hole in the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, 'Well, that was a lot of fuss for a fancy autocomplete.' I'd probably post something cheeky online. I'm one of the people who really expected more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it changes very little. I'd keep using the tools I already use, keep teaching on Thursdays, retire around 63. I'd be a bit disappointed, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am, really. I'd keep pushing the useful tools at the depot, like the fault-mapping app, because they do save the lads time. We've got about three months of bills saved, and I'd keep chipping away at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit let down. Like a film everyone said was amazing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use an AI assistant every day. What does it actually help with?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It writes the job packs and the risk assessments, it checks the old cable maps against the new ones, and it helps me prepare my Thursday lessons. Last month it spotted that a map from 1974 had a joint in the wrong street, which saved us digging up the wrong pavement. It's not magic, but it's a good apprentice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it all stays like this, what do your last years look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a lot like now, with more teaching. I'd like to do two nights a week at the college when I slow down. Mariam keeps saying I'll never fully retire, and she's probably right.

S0.say: He'd say AI was a lot of fuss for a fancy autocomplete, and he'd probably post something cheeky about it online. He admits he's one of the people who expected more.
S0.think: It changes very little for him: he'd keep using the tools he has, keep teaching and retire around 63. He'd be a bit disappointed.
S0.do: Carries on as now and keeps pushing useful tools like the fault-mapping app at the depot. Keeps adding slowly to savings that cover about three months of bills.
S0.feel: Calm and a little let down, like a much-praised film that didn't deliver.
S0.quote: It's not magic, but it's a good apprentice.
S0.fieldNote: Colin is the early adopter of his depot and uses AI every day for job packs and old cable maps. He's mildly disappointed by a plateau rather than relieved. His teaching at the college is clearly where he sees his future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good if we steer it and bad if we don't. The tools should take the paperwork off us so we can do more of the skilled work, and the union should make sure that's how it goes. I'd say it at work and at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. I'm already ahead with the tools, and the company's going to need people who can do the joint and use the software. It's the people who won't touch it I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the company to let me run a training session for the crews on the tools, starting in the first few months. I'd take a short robotics or automation course at the college myself, probably in the evenings. And I'd get the union to write the training into the pay deal so it's paid time, not people's weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. Even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the depot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners and the older lads who hate screens. There's a guy, Des, 61, best jointer I ever worked with, and he can't stand his phone. If the job changes around him, he'll just walk out, and we'd lose forty years of knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you see any new job in this for yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I can see a role in the middle, someone who knows the cables and knows the software, training both people and machines. If nobody's doing that job yet, I'd want to invent it.

S1.say: He'd say AI is good if it's steered and bad if it isn't: the tools should take paperwork away so crews can do more skilled work, and the union should make sure of that. He'd say it at work and at the college.
S1.think: He honestly thinks it's good for him, since he's already ahead with the tools and the company will need people who can joint cable and use software. He'd worry about colleagues who won't touch it.
S1.do: Asks to run training sessions on the tools for crews in the first few months and takes an evening robotics or automation course. Gets the union to put paid training into the pay deal.
S1.feel: Mostly calm, even a bit excited.
S1.quote: If nobody's doing that job yet, I'd want to invent it.
S1.fieldNote: This picture suits him, and he sees a bridging role for himself between crews and software. His progressive streak shows in wanting training to be paid time written into the pay deal. His worry is for Des, a gifted jointer who can't stand screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to act like it's a war: income support now, public control of how robots are used on the grid, and no company firing thousands overnight. I'd say it loudly, and I'd be helping the union put together a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not the robots that worry me, it's the chaos. If AI can do almost anything in two years, then my edge with the tools stops mattering. Everyone's equal again, and I'm 60 with three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder this month, maybe double what we put in now, and I'd stop the kitchen we'd planned. I'd apply for any role running or checking robot crews the moment the company advertised one, because better to be inside the change. And I'd work with the union on a deal for older workers and lobby our city councillors about public oversight of grid robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about the tech and scared about the speed, both at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're good with the tools. Why would two years still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because being early only helps if there's time for being early to pay off. With two years, the machines learn faster than I can stay ahead of them. My advantage is maybe eighteen months, and then it's gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Mariam do with money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen goes first, that's easy. Then we'd look at whether Mariam goes full-time again, nurses might be safer for longer, who knows. We'd also tell Nadia we can't help as much with the last bit of her degree, which would be a hard conversation.

S2.say: He'd say governments should act as if it's a war: income support now, public control over how robots are used on the grid, and no company firing thousands overnight. He'd say it loudly and help the union build a plan.
S2.think: It's the chaos that worries him, not the robots. If AI can do almost anything in two years, his edge with the tools stops mattering, and he'd be 60 with three months of savings.
S2.do: Doubles his monthly savings and cancels the planned kitchen. Applies for any role running or checking robot crews as soon as it's advertised, works with the union on a deal for older workers and lobbies city councillors on public oversight of grid robots.
S2.feel: Anxious, excited by the technology and scared by the speed at the same time.
S2.quote: My advantage is maybe eighteen months, and then it's gone.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-forward of crews loses its edge in a two-year timeline, and he sees that clearly. His response mixes moving into the change himself with strong collective and political demands. He'd also cut back on helping his daughter, which clearly pains him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly, if we start tomorrow. Retraining paid for by the companies, a seat for workers on the decisions, and a guarantee for people close to retirement. I'd say it at the college too, to the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is about right. I'd be 63 when it lands, and I'd have time to move into training or robot supervision before the crews shrink. I'd go out on my own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do a proper certificate in robotics maintenance at the college, evenings, about a year long. I'd offer to run the company's pilot with robot crews on the cable side. And I'd take on more teaching, paid, as a second income for when I slow down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but there's a plan in it. I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach your Thursday class in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to work alongside the machines, honestly. How to check a robot's joint, how to spot when the software's wrong about an old map. The craft doesn't disappear overnight, it just moves from your hands to your eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version of this where you come out ahead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, yes. If I'm the guy who knows both the cables and the robots, I'm useful until the very end. But I don't want to come out ahead while Des and the others get dumped, that's not a win.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to do it properly if work starts tomorrow, with company-paid retraining, worker seats on decisions and a guarantee for people near retirement. He'd say it to his students too.
S3.think: Five years feels about right to him: he'd be 63 when it lands, with time to move into training or robot supervision first. He'd go out on his own terms.
S3.do: Takes a year-long evening certificate in robotics maintenance and offers to run the company's robot crew pilot on the cable side. Takes on more paid teaching as a second income.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but steadied by having a plan.
S3.quote: The craft doesn't disappear overnight, it just moves from your hands to your eyes.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives him room to turn his early adoption into a real role. He's hungry to lead the pilot, yet he refuses to count it as a win if older colleagues are left behind. The idea of the craft moving from hands to eyes was striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd better not waste it. I'd want a national plan, retraining in every trade, and a share of the gains going to the people whose work the robots take. I'd be cheerful about it, but pushy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good news. I'd be retired by the time it fully lands, and in the meantime I'd have years to help shape how it happens on the grid. Honestly, I'd enjoy that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep using the new tools as they come, and in a few years put my hand up to lead the company's robot programme on the cable side. I'd teach more at the college as I slow down. Money-wise, nothing dramatic, just steady saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Curious more than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sami and Nadia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sami's in software, so he'll feel it before me, and I'd tell him to start planning now while he's young. Nadia, with law, I don't know. I'd tell them both that ten years is a long time if you use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'll be 68 in 2036. Would you still be working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a day or two a week, teaching or checking robot work. Mariam says I'll be the old man down the hole with a tablet telling the robot it's doing it wrong. She's not wrong.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is a gift that mustn't be wasted, calling for a national plan, retraining in every trade and a share of the gains for people whose work robots take. He'd be cheerful about it but pushy.
S4.think: It's mostly good news for him: he'd be retired when it fully lands and would have years to help shape it on the grid. He'd enjoy that.
S4.do: Keeps working and using new tools, then volunteers to lead the company's robot programme on the cable side in a few years. Teaches more at the college as he slows down, with steady saving.
S4.feel: Mostly calm, curious more than worried.
S4.quote: Mariam says I'll be the old man down the hole with a tablet telling the robot it's doing it wrong.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he's relaxed and sees himself shaping the change rather than suffering it. His worry moves to his son in software. He imagines working a day or two a week well into his late 60s, which fits his love of the craft.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because everything moves faster than anyone can keep up, even people like me who like the stuff. What would help is income support for older workers during the switch, and a real say for unions in how robots come onto the grid. And free night courses, I'd be first in the queue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who teaches the machines. Every robot on a cable job is going to learn from somebody's work, probably from guys like Des. If our knowledge builds these things, we should get something back for it, not just a handshake and a leaving card.

headlineQuote: If our knowledge builds these things, we should get something back for it, not just a handshake and a leaving card.
portrait: Colin Farah is a 58-year-old underground cable crew lead in the city who uses an AI assistant every day and teaches cable jointing on Thursday nights. He's mildly disappointed if AI plateaus and actually energised by steady disruption, seeing a new bridging role between crews and machines. A two-year path to AGI makes him anxious because his head start with the tools would vanish, and he'd be 60 with three months of savings. With five or ten years he plans a robotics certificate, more teaching and a lead role in robot pilots, while pushing hard through the union and politics so older colleagues like Des aren't dumped.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it moves faster than anyone can keep up with, even people who like the technology.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for older workers during the switch, a real union say in how robots come onto the grid, and free night courses.
